Fork-tailed sunbird (Aethopyga christinae) neonates emerge from eggs with a remarkably low body mass, with field measurements indicating an initial wet weight of just 0.9 grams [Ww0 = 0.9 grams]. This altricial hatchling mass, based on comparisons with the congener Aethopyga siparaja, represents a tiny fraction of the ultimate adult size that will be attained. Eggs incubated at a temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] hatch after a relatively short developmental period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a duration consistent with the rapid embryogenesis observed in many small-bodied passerines. This abbreviated incubation period is ecologically advantageous in tropical environments where nest predation pressure is often elevated, allowing parents to reduce the cumulative risk to the brood. Following hatching, the helpless, blind chicks are entirely dependent on their parents for warmth and food, initiating a period of intensive provisioning that will fuel their subsequent growth towards fledging and independence.

Adult female Fork-tailed sunbirds reach an ultimate wet weight of 5.8 grams [Wwi = 5.8 grams], a diminutive size that places them among the smallest nectarivorous birds in Southeast Asia. This low body mass is typical of the genus Aethopyga and reflects a life history strategy centred on high metabolic rates and rapid energy turnover. Under the ambient thermal conditions typically experienced during active foraging periods in their subtropical range (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), measurements of basal oxygen consumption have produced a value of 21.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 21.5 milliliters per hour]. This elevated metabolic rate is characteristic of hummingbird-like nectarivores, which must process large volumes of dilute sugar water to meet their daily energetic demands, a physiological constraint that fundamentally shapes their foraging behaviour, activity patterns, and overall life history pace.

Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], several critical developmental and life history milestones have been documented for the Fork-tailed sunbird, drawing on data from the closely related Aethopyga siparaja. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and the young bird's first departure from the nest, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is followed by a longer interval before sexual maturation, with puberty being attained at 57 days after hatching [tp = 57 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This two-to-three-month delay between fledging and reproductive competence likely reflects the time required for juvenile birds to refine their foraging skills, develop flight proficiency, and complete the final stages of somatic growth necessary to support the high energetic costs of breeding, including territory defence and courtship feeding.

Reproductive output in the Fork-tailed sunbird is constrained by both body size and environmental seasonality. Females typically produce a clutch of three eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of three eggs], and available records indicate that they initiate only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. The maximum lifespan recorded for the Fork-tailed sunbird, based on data from long-term mark-recapture studies of the congener Aethopyga siparaja, is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under the same thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic period (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]). This relatively short longevity is consistent with the fast-paced life history of small nectarivorous birds, characterized by high metabolic demands, elevated predation risk, and substantial energetic investments in each breeding attempt.
